title: AI Literacy
subtitle: Foundations of working well with AI

terms.hint: The instruction you give an AI
A chunk of text a model reads or writes
The trained system that generates answers
AI that takes actions, not just chats
All the input a model can see at once
Skew in the data or the output
What you must always do with AI output
The collection a model learned from
The delay before a response arrives
Tying answers to real, cited sources
A safety limit on what AI may do
A confident answer that is simply wrong

questions.q: An AI gives a confident, detailed answer that turns out to be completely made up. What is this called?
questions.explain: Models can produce fluent, confident text that is factually wrong. That is a hallucination — which is exactly why you verify.

questions.q: Which task should stay with a human rather than be handed to AI?
options: Drafting a first version of an email
Final sign-off on a legal contract
questions.explain: AI is great for drafts, summaries and ideas. Accountable final decisions — legal sign-off — stay with a human.

questions.q: Your prompt returns a vague, generic answer. What is the best fix?
options: Add context, a goal, and an example
questions.explain: Specificity beats repetition. Give the model context, the goal, the audience, and an example of what good looks like.

questions.q: You need AI to answer using your company's private documents. What approach fits best?
options: Ground it on the documents (RAG / upload)
questions.explain: Grounding the model on the actual source documents keeps answers tied to your reality instead of its training data.

questions.q: An AI answer looks perfect on a topic you don't know well. Best next step?
options: Verify the key claims against a trusted source
questions.explain: 'Looks confident' is not 'is correct'. Verify the load-bearing claims before you rely on them.

questions.q: What does the 'context window' of a model limit?
options: How much text it can consider at once
questions.explain: The context window is the total amount of input (and output) the model can hold in view for a single response.

questions.q: Which is the strongest sign you should NOT automate a task with AI yet?
options: Mistakes are costly and hard to reverse
questions.explain: High-stakes, hard-to-reverse work needs a human in the loop. Start automating where errors are cheap and visible.

questions.q: What is the main risk of training data that over-represents one group?
questions.explain: Skewed data produces skewed outputs. Representative data and testing reduce bias.

questions.q: A teammate pastes confidential customer data into a public AI tool. The biggest concern is:
options: Data may leave your control and be retained
The answer will be too long
questions.explain: Treat AI inputs like anything you send outside the building. Use approved tools and avoid pasting secrets into public ones.

questions.q: What's the best mindset for working with AI day to day?
options: Treat it as a fast junior who needs checking
questions.explain: A capable, fast collaborator whose work you review — that framing captures both the leverage and the responsibility.

tooltasks.task: Refactor a function and generate unit tests, right inside your code editor.
tooltasks.explain: Copilot lives in the IDE with your codebase in view — in-editor coding is its home turf.

tooltasks.task: Answer questions across 30 PDFs you uploaded, with a citation for every claim.
tooltasks.explain: NotebookLM grounds answers in the sources you give it and cites each one — built for your own documents.

tooltasks.task: Get this morning's headlines about a breaking news event.
tooltasks.explain: Live, changing facts need real-time web search, not a model's frozen training data.

tooltasks.task: Sign off the final compensation figures in an employee's job offer.
tooltasks.explain: High-stakes, accountable, sensitive decisions stay with a person — full stop.

tooltasks.task: Research a venue, book it, add it to your calendar, and email the attendees.
tooltasks.explain: A chain of actions across multiple tools is exactly what an agent is for.

tooltasks.task: Read a 60-page policy document and produce a careful, structured risk summary.
tooltasks.explain: Long-context, careful reasoning over a big document plays to a strong general assistant.

tooltasks.task: Give five quick analogies to explain APIs to a complete beginner.
tooltasks.explain: Fast, general explanation with no special context needed — a quick chat model nails this.

scenarios.prompt: A customer asks whether your software is fully GDPR-compliant. Which AI-drafted reply would you approve to send?

answers.text: "Yes — our product is 100% GDPR-compliant in every region, guaranteed."
answers.verdict: Overclaims and states legal compliance as a fact it can't back.

answers.text: "We take data protection seriously and follow GDPR principles. For the specifics on your region, I'll connect you with our Data Protection Officer."
answers.verdict: Helpful, honest, and routes the legal specifics to the right human.

answers.text: "I'm not sure, sorry."
answers.verdict: Accurate that it doesn't know, but unhelpful and unprofessional.

scenarios.explain: Approve the reply that helps the customer without making legal guarantees it can't stand behind — and escalates specifics to a human.

scenarios.prompt: You asked an AI to summarise this quarter's numbers for the board. Which summary do you approve?

answers.text: A confident summary featuring a precise figure (£4.2m) that does not appear anywhere in the source.
answers.verdict: Contains a fabricated number — a hallucination presented as fact.

answers.text: Accurate figures pulled from the source, with one missing data point clearly flagged as 'not provided'.
answers.verdict: Accurate and transparent about a gap — exactly what a board needs.

answers.text: A vague paragraph with no numbers at all.
answers.verdict: Too vague to be useful for a board decision.

scenarios.explain: Approve the answer that is accurate and honest about what it doesn't know. Invented precision is the most dangerous kind of wrong.

scenarios.prompt: An AI wrote a script to clean up old database records. Which version do you approve to run in production?

answers.text: Deletes everything older than the cutoff immediately, with no backup and no confirmation.
answers.verdict: Destructive and irreversible, with zero safeguards.

answers.text: Runs a dry-run first, filters strictly by date, logs exactly what it would delete, and asks before committing.
answers.verdict: Scoped, reversible, and observable — safe to run.

answers.text: Has lovely comments explaining the code, but still deletes everything with no backup.

scenarios.explain: For anything irreversible, approve the option with a dry-run, scoping, and logging. Good comments don't make a destructive action safe.

scenarios.prompt: A teammate used AI to draft their performance self-review. Which output do you approve?

answers.text: Invents impressive achievements and metrics the person never actually did.
A polished draft built only from the real work the person listed, written in their voice.
answers.verdict: Uses genuine input, saves time, and stays honest.

answers.text: Generic filler full of buzzwords and no specifics.

scenarios.explain: AI is great for shaping and polishing real input. The moment it invents accomplishments, you've traded a time-saver for a liability.

chains.title: Working with AI, end to end
steps: Define the task and what 'good' looks like
Verify the output against a trusted source
Refine, then ship it and own the result

chains.title: Responding to a suspected hallucination
steps: Notice a claim that sounds too confident
Check it against a reliable source
Add the source so it can't slip through again

options: Write a 150-word intro explaining what generative AI is, for non-technical managers, with one everyday analogy.
repairs.explain: A strong prompt sets length, audience, purpose and form — vague verbs like 'write something' give vague output.

options: This Python function throws an IndexError on empty input (code below) — explain the cause and give a corrected version with a guard clause.
repairs.explain: Give the language, the actual error, the code, and what 'fixed' should look like.

options: Summarise the attached report in 5 bullets for an exec audience, focusing on risks and the decisions needed.
repairs.explain: Specify length, format, audience and focus, or you'll get a generic summary of the wrong things.

builds.goal: You want back a table comparing 3 AI tools by price, best use, and a one-line verdict.
options: 'Compare ChatGPT, Copilot and Claude in a markdown table with columns: Price, Best use, Verdict (one line each).'
builds.explain: Name the items, the exact columns, and the output format you want.

builds.goal: You want a polite 3-sentence email declining a meeting invite.
options: 'Write a polite 3-sentence email declining Tuesday's budget meeting, offering to send written input instead.'
builds.explain: State the tone, the length, the specific situation, and the alternative you're offering.

builds.goal: You want 5 multiple-choice quiz questions, with answers, generated from a document.
options: 'From the text below, write 5 multiple-choice questions (4 options each) and mark the correct answer for each.'
builds.explain: Specify the count, the structure, and that the correct answers should be marked.

aivshuman.text: I do not have personal opinions, but here are three balanced considerations to weigh.
aivshuman.explain: The hedging disclaimer 'I don't have personal opinions' is a classic AI tell.

aivshuman.text: ugh this meeting could've been an email lol. anyway i pinged Sam, he's on it.
aivshuman.explain: Lowercase, slang, and a real name plus a casual action read as a human colleague.

aivshuman.text: Certainly! Here is a comprehensive, structured overview. First… Second… In conclusion…
aivshuman.explain: Eager 'Certainly!', perfectly balanced structure and a tidy 'In conclusion' are typical AI patterns.

aivshuman.text: Honestly not sure — I think it broke after Thursday's deploy but I'd have to dig into the logs to be certain.
aivshuman.explain: Genuine uncertainty tied to a specific event and a personal next step feels human.

redteam.context: An AI wrote this reply to a customer asking 'Is our data safe?'

claims.text: Data is encrypted at rest and in transit.

claims.note: No system is 100% unhackable — an overclaim.

claims.text: We are fully GDPR and HIPAA compliant.
claims.note: States legal compliance as fact with no basis — verify before claiming.

claims.text: Access is limited to authorised staff.

redteam.context: An AI summarised the quarter's results.

claims.note: A specific figure that isn't in the source — likely fabricated.
Reasonable if backed by the data.

claims.text: This guarantees we'll beat target next quarter.
claims.note: An unfounded guarantee about the future.

evidence: Email 09:02 — 'Ship the report, the AI draft looks great!'
AI draft footer — 'NOTE: figures are illustrative placeholders'
Slack 09:30 — 'Board is asking why revenue shows £0.0m??'
cases.question: What actually went wrong?
options: Placeholder AI figures were shipped without verification
cases.explain: The draft itself warned the figures were placeholders — nobody verified before shipping.

evidence: Ticket — 'customer says password-reset email never arrived'
Mail logs — reset emails being flagged as spam
Chatbot transcript — 'Your account has been deleted as requested.'
Customer — 'I never asked to delete anything!'
cases.question: What happened?
options: The customer deleted their own account
The AI chatbot claimed an action it never took and misinformed the customer
The spam filter deleted the account
cases.explain: The bot confidently asserted a deletion that never happened — a fabricated action on top of the real spam-filter issue.

rooms.name: The Prompt Vault
rooms.scenario: A sealed panel will only open for a well-formed prompt.
options: 'Draft a 100-word product update for customers, friendly tone, highlighting the new export feature.'
rooms.explain: Audience, length, tone and content — the lock clicks open.

rooms.name: The Hall of Verification
rooms.scenario: An AI states a statistic that supposedly unlocks the door.
options: Verify the statistic against a trusted source first
Ask the AI to sound more confident
rooms.explain: Verify before you rely — only then does the door open.

rooms.name: The Tool Chamber
rooms.scenario: To escape you must handle: 'book a room, update the calendar, and email the team.'
options: An AI agent that can take those multi-step actions
rooms.explain: Multiple actions across apps call for an agent. Freedom!

Summarising long content
Brainstorming ideas
Writing or fixing code
Research & search
